clue.text: Old coppers went by foot

parts.note: reads as old-time policemen walking the beat, but describes a pedal-driven Victorian bicycle named after two old copper coins of different sizes

explanation.walkthrough: Coppers are pre-decimal British copper coins as well as police officers; the high-wheeled bicycle was named after the large penny and tiny farthing, and its rider propelled it with the feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description of the old high-wheeled bicycle, named after two copper coins and pedalled by foot.

clue.text: Changing role in era that's past

indicators.note: changing tells us to alter the arrangement of the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone's role is shifting within an era that is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing' rearranges ROLE IN ERA.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happened earlier on lies in the past, so the adverbial phrase matches 'past' used adverbially.

clue.text: Like the accent of US space admin figure?

parts.note: NASA is the US space administration
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a figure

explanation.surface: A question about whether an official at the American space agency speaks with a twang.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark hints that a nasal twang is the stereotyped American accent.
explanation.definitionFit: A nasal accent is one voiced through the nose, a common description of an American twang.

clue.text: Quaker's companions?

parts.note: a Quaker belongs to the Religious Society of ..., so fellow members are both companions and co-religionists

explanation.definitionFit: Companions are pals, and members of the Quaker movement are formally called by this same name.

clue.text: When students make merry music

parts.note: a rag is a British student charity carnival of pranks and fun
a time answers the question when

explanation.surface: Student party season is when this jaunty music plays.
explanation.walkthrough: Rag week is the British student custom of fundraising stunts and revelry.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragtime is a syncopated piano music style popular around 1900.

clue.text: Travelled free to Oxford, say, and got married

parts.note: to hitch is to hitch-hike, travelling free by thumbing lifts
students go up to a university such as Oxford

explanation.surface: Someone thumbed a lift to Oxford and then wed.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage one goes 'up' to Oxford or Cambridge when starting university.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting hitched is an informal idiom for getting married.

clue.text: Two Poles about to come up with nothing? Untrue

indicators.note: about means the pole letters sit around the next piece

parts.note: N and S are the north and south poles

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means reading the word to from bottom to top

parts.note: O is the zero shape for nothing

explanation.surface: Two Polish people are about to rise with nothing, which is false.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland but means compass points; in a down clue 'come up' reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'not so' denies a claim, declaring it untrue.

clue.text: Trousseaux for painters of nudes?

definitions.meaning: a bride's collected linen and clothes, traditionally kept in the lowest drawer of a chest
artists who sketch naked models draw backsides

explanation.definitionFit: A bottom drawer is a British term for a trousseau; humorously, those who draw bottoms are the artists.

clue.text: Three caroused, when involved in a bit of a domestic row

definitions.text: a bit of a domestic row

indicators.note: involved means twisted up, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Three people have been carousing and get mixed up in a household quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges THREE CAROUSED. 'Domestic row' looks like a family argument but means a row of homes.
explanation.definitionFit: A terraced house is one dwelling within a continuous row of joined homes.

clue.text: Disturbed rhino and gnus stampeding

indicators.note: disturbed means thrown into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rhino is upset and wildebeest charge across the plain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbed' rearranges RHINO and GNUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Onrushing means surging forward headlong, as a stampeding herd does.

clue.text: Cut of the cloth?

parts.note: the cloth is the clergy, and their cut is the share of produce owed to the church

explanation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' is a traditional term for the clergy; 'cut' means a share, not tailoring.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe was the tenth of income paid to support the church, the clergy's share.

clue.text: Difficulty in hearing

definitions.meaning: a trouble or ordeal that tests someone
a court hearing of a case

explanation.definitionFit: A trial is both a hardship that tests one and a court case heard before a judge.

clue.text: Hour being struck for close acquaintance

indicators.note: struck suggests being knocked about, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A clock chimes the hour for a close friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'struck' rearranges HOUR BEING; it reads as a clock chiming.
explanation.definitionFit: A neighbour lives close by and is usually someone you know.

clue.text: They're not real instances of motorway madness

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's first motorway, with the 1 read as the letter I
rages are fits of madness or fury

explanation.surface: Road-rage incidents on a motorway are illusory.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is a major British motorway from London to Leeds; the digit 1 doubles as I.
explanation.definitionFit: Mirages are optical illusions, things seen that are not really there.

clue.text: Makes teenagers obstreperous

indicators.note: obstreperous means unruly, so the letters of the word teenagers are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something causes adolescents to become rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'obstreperous' rearranges TEENAGERS.
explanation.definitionFit: To generate is to produce or create, the same as makes.

clue.text: Sort of disease treated by district nurses?

definitions.text: Sort of disease treated by district nurses?

parts.words: Sort of disease treated by district nurses?
parts.note: district nurses are British community nurses, but the joke is a disease confined to one district or locality

explanation.walkthrough: District nurses are British community nurses who visit patients at home.
explanation.definitionFit: An endemic disease is one regularly found in a particular region or population.

clue.text: Much rain about a part of China

indicators.note: about means turned around, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wet province in the Far East gets plenty of rainfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals the rearrangement while the surface makes it mean 'around a part of China'.
explanation.definitionFit: Manchuria is a historic region of north-east China.

clue.text: Came across an intro that's different

indicators.note: different means changed, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone found an unusual opening section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' rearranges AN INTRO.
explanation.definitionFit: To run into someone is to encounter them by chance, to come across them.

clue.text: Daily prayers for those suffering from Oedipus complex?

indicators.note: complex means intricate or tangled, so the letters of this name are rearranged

explanation.surface: Prayers for patients with a Freudian fixation on their mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complex' rearranges OEDIPUS, while seeming to complete 'Oedipus complex'.
explanation.definitionFit: Opus Dei, the work of God, is a monastic term for the daily round of liturgical prayer.

clue.text: I write in red, not green

indicators.note: in places the first pieces within the colour word

parts.note: to pen is to write

explanation.surface: A teacher marks work in red ink, never green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red' looks like a teacher's ink colour but is the container; 'green' means unripe, not the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Green fruit is unripe, so something not green has ripened.

clue.text: Saw work that's splendid

definitions.meaning: cutting wood along the grain with a ripsaw

explanation.definitionFit: Ripping is sawing wood along the grain, and also dated British slang for excellent.

clue.text: Dampcourse laid across another sort of course

definitions.text: Dampcourse laid across another sort of course

parts.words: Dampcourse laid across another sort of course
parts.note: a damp course is building waterproofing, but here it is a wet obstacle placed across a racecourse

explanation.walkthrough: A damp-course is a waterproof layer in a wall; the clue splits it to describe a wet hazard on a steeplechase track.
explanation.definitionFit: A water jump is a steeplechase obstacle of water that horses or runners must leap.

clue.text: Large cat making a row about midnight

indicators.note: about means the row word goes round the letter

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
G is the middle letter of night

explanation.surface: A big cat starts a commotion around twelve at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Midnight' is read as the middle of 'night', G; 'row' means tier, not a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: The tiger is the largest of the big cats.

clue.text: Swift portrayal of a rude lout

definitions.text: Swift portrayal of a rude lout

parts.words: Swift portrayal of a rude lout
parts.note: Jonathan Swift depicted brutish human-like creatures in Gulliver's Travels

explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' is the author Jonathan Swift, not a speedy sketch.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's brutish creatures gave English a word for a coarse, boorish person.

clue.text: Old friends are unlikely to meet at this club

definitions.text: Old friends are unlikely to meet at this club

parts.words: Old friends are unlikely to meet at this club
parts.note: elderly people would not gather at a club meant for teenagers

explanation.walkthrough: A youth club is a British community centre for teenagers.
explanation.definitionFit: Clubs for young people exclude the elderly, so aged friends would not meet there.

clue.text: Appropriate ceremonial form in speech

indicators.note: in speech means we hear the word rather than read it

parts.note: a rite is a ceremonial form

explanation.walkthrough: RITE and RIGHT sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Right means fitting or proper, just as appropriate does.

clue.text: Girl had to change a quid before getting the drinks

indicators.note: to change means to alter, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: Iris is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl had to break a pound note before buying the cocktails.
explanation.walkthrough: A quid is British slang for a pound; 'to change' looks like making change for money but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Daiquiris are rum cocktails made with lime and sugar.

clue.text: Advancement crucial to a school principal

parts.note: pressing means urgent or crucial
a head is a head teacher of a school

explanation.surface: Promotion matters greatly to a headteacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advancement' is read as the act of moving on.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing ahead means moving forward determinedly, an act of advancement.
